paras: The shooting of William Brown was an incident in Carlin, Nevada, in mid-1895, in which Constable Cozzens shot Brown, whom the local paper described as "the colored man." Brown survived, was indicted for burglary, pleaded guilty, and was sentenced to two years in the penitentiary in early August 1895. The shooting is known only from a single sentence in an Elko newspaper's local column.

According to the Elko Daily Independent of 7 August 1895, Brown had been shot by Constable Cozzens in Carlin "a few weeks ago," placing the shooting in roughly July 1895. The paper gave no account of why or how the constable fired, where Brown was hit, or how badly he was hurt. Because Brown was later indicted for burglary, the shooting may have occurred during an arrest or pursuit, but the item does not say so.

On about 6 August 1895, Brown pleaded guilty to the indictment charging him with burglary. Judge Cheney sentenced him to two years in the penitentiary. No report of any inquiry into the constable's use of his weapon appears in the coverage.

The Daily Independent ran the item as one line in its "Salmagundi" miscellany, among notes on the Ruby Valley hay crop, gold shipments to Europe and a Denver bank failure. The shooting served only to identify the defendant, and the paper offered no comment on it. The Weekly Independent reprinted the sentence unchanged on 11 August under the heading "From Wednesday's Daily."
No other white paper and no Black newspaper in the coverage carried the shooting or the sentencing.
